## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no trials yet. The starting architecture scored 0.000 on both seeds, so it either cannot learn exact builds within budget, or the recipe gives it too few policy updates. The default recipe uses 4096 samples per update, so there are only about 32 PPO updates in 131k steps. To place a brick correctly, the agent has to learn three things: the brick's landing layer (the highest filled cell under its footprint), whether that layer's target cells are all missing, and whether placing it would seal missing cells below. The starting network collapses the layer dimension early with 1x1 convolutions, which makes this per-layer comparison hard. In round 1, all three candidates use the same recipe with more frequent updates (smaller batches, 3 epochs, longer horizon), so differences between them come from the architecture. Candidate A changes only the recipe and is the control. B adds an explicit layer-token head. C tests global attention.

### Round 2
All four architectures (the baseline, a recipe-only change, layer tokens and attention) scored exactly 0 on dev and 0 on training success. So the 2-seed results cannot rank any of them. When even sampled training never reaches an exact build, the likely limit is the training signal and the number of samples, not small differences between networks. With the default recipe the run gets about 32 PPO updates of 4 epochs. Setting ppo_epochs=1 roughly triples the sample budget (about 426k steps at r=1), and with 128 envs it gives about 200 updates. Lower entropy should help commit to precise actions among 257 options. So this round keeps one recipe (1 epoch, lr 2e-3, entropy 0.003) across three networks: the baseline, which tests whether the recipe alone gets above 0; a layer-token head with cumulative 'below/above' summaries, which match the landing-layer structure; and a deeper dilated CNN, which tests capacity against sample count.

### Round 3
All 6 trials score exactly 0 on dev and 0 on training success, across every network and recipe tried. That includes 1 epoch with 400k samples, 3 epochs, attention, layer tokens and a dilated CNN. A change of this size should leave some mark, so the cause is probably systematic, not seed noise or capacity. One thing every trial shares is the hand-built footprint pool head. It assumes the anchor is the top-left corner and that footprints are (dy, dx) as described. The task warns that the world may differ from its description. If the action geometry differs (transposed footprints or another anchor corner), every placement score is misaligned. The agent could then fill most of the target but almost never build it exactly. The next tests drop that assumption: a learned 3x3 action head, the legality mask as an input (its edges show each brick's extent), and a pool head that covers every anchor and orientation.

### Round 4
All nine trials scored exactly 0 on dev, and training success in the last 10% of training was also 0. The changes covered three recipes (3 epochs, 1 epoch with high samples, and low gamma with low lr), three trunks (a CNN, layer tokens and a transformer) and three heads (footprint pooling, a learned 3x3 conv and multi-anchor pooling). A uniform zero across such different designs points to a shared assumption, not to capacity or recipe. Every head so far assumes that action index = type*Y*X + y*X + x and maps the logits spatially onto the grid. The task warns that the world may differ from its description. If the action layout or footprint geometry differs, for example cell-major order, transposed axes or reordered types, every spatial head is wrong. This round tests heads that assume no action geometry: a fully connected head to all actions, with the legality mask fed in through a learned linear layer, so the network can learn the real layout.
